plan.contextChunk: This figure places two geometric constructions side by side, labeled (a) and (b), both concerning light leaving a pair of narrow slits. In (a) a vertical tan bar at the left represents the slit barrier, with its two openings marked S1 and S2 and their separation bracketed as d. A gray vertical bar at the right is labeled Screen, and the horizontal gap between barrier and screen is bracketed below as D. Two teal rays, r1 from S1 and r2 from S2, each carrying a short drawn wave train, converge on a black dot labeled P on the screen. A dashed horizontal line runs from the midpoint between the slits to the point C on the screen, the vertical offset from C up to P is bracketed as y, and a dashed line from the slit midpoint to P makes the angle theta with that horizontal. Panel (b) magnifies the region just beyond the barrier: the same two openings, again separated by d, send rays now drawn parallel, each labeled to P and each inclined at theta to its own dashed reference. A dashed segment runs from the upper slit onto the lower ray at a marked right angle, isolating the short extra stretch labeled delta l. Enlarging the near-slit geometry beside the full layout shows that only the small difference delta l, not the lengths of r1 and r2 themselves, decides how the waves combine at P.

interactionPlan.concept: For two-slit interference, the only thing that determines whether light arriving at a point P on the screen interferes constructively or destructively is the tiny extra path length Δl = d·sinθ travelled by the far slit's ray, not the individual path lengths r₁ and r₂.
elements: Panel (a) label beneath the left construction; panel (b) label beneath the right construction
Left panel: vertical tan/ochre bar representing the slit barrier with two gaps
Slit labels S₁ (upper) and S₂ (lower) with small black tick marks
Vertical double-headed arrow bracket on the far left labeled d spanning S₁ to S₂
Gray vertical bar on the right labeled 'Screen'
Horizontal double-headed arrow bracket below labeled D spanning barrier to screen
Teal ray r₁ from S₁ to point P with mid-ray arrowhead and label r₁
Teal ray r₂ from S₂ to point P with mid-ray arrowhead and label r₂
Short sinusoidal wave trains drawn on each teal ray near the slits
Black filled dot on the screen labeled P
Dashed horizontal center line from the slit midpoint to the screen, ending at labeled point C
Dashed straight line from slit midpoint to P (the bisector ray)
Angle arc labeled θ between the dashed horizontal and the dashed midpoint-to-P line
Vertical double-headed arrow bracket on the right labeled y spanning C up to P
Right panel: same tan barrier bar with two slit gaps, vertical bracket labeled d
Two parallel teal rays leaving the slits at angle θ, each with an arrowhead and the label 'to P'
Dashed horizontal reference lines from each slit with angle arcs labeled θ
Dashed segment from the upper slit dropped perpendicular onto the lower ray, with a right-angle square marker
Dashed segment from the upper slit continuing to close the small right triangle
Short double-headed arrow along the lower ray labeled Δl marking the extra path length
Readout annotation showing current values of y, θ, d, Δl and Δl/λ (order m)
Constructive/destructive indicator text tied to whether Δl is a whole or half number of wavelengths

interactions.teaches: Moving the observation point P up the screen increases the angle θ, which in turn lengthens the extra path Δl — so position on the screen and path difference are two views of the same quantity.
interactions.label: Height of P on screen, y (mm)

interactions.teaches: For a fixed viewing angle, widening the slits scales the extra path length in direct proportion, making Δl = d·sinθ visible as a geometric fact rather than a formula.
interactions.label: Slit separation d (µm)

interactions.teaches: The full apparatus shows two long, slightly unequal paths; the near-slit magnification shows that their entire difference is captured by one short right-triangle leg — the far-field approximation that makes interference tractable.
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Each geometric quantity (d, D, y, θ, r₁, r₂, Δl) names a specific segment or angle in the construction, so the symbols in the formula map onto real pieces of the picture.

demo_steps.title: The apparatus
demo_steps.narration: Light leaves two slits separated by d and travels a distance D to the screen. Choose a point P a height y above the center point C; the rays r₁ and r₂ reach it along slightly different paths.

demo_steps.title: Slide P up the screen
demo_steps.narration: Drag P upward. The angle θ between the center line and the line to P grows, and r₁ becomes noticeably shorter than r₂ — but the difference is far too small to see at this scale.

demo_steps.title: Zoom in on the slits
demo_steps.narration: Because D is enormous compared with d, the two rays to P are essentially parallel. Dropping a perpendicular from the upper slit onto the lower ray isolates the whole difference in one short segment, Δl.

demo_steps.title: Read the right triangle
demo_steps.narration: The triangle has hypotenuse d and the angle at the slit equals θ, so the isolated leg is exactly Δl = d·sinθ. Watch it shrink as you move P back toward the center.

demo_steps.title: Widen the slits
demo_steps.narration: Hold the angle and widen d: Δl grows in direct proportion, so more bright fringes are packed into the same span of screen.

demo_steps.title: Both views at once
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, a screen-scale change in y and a micron-scale change in Δl move together. Whenever Δl is a whole number of wavelengths the waves arrive in phase and P is bright; a half-integer gives darkness.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The kilometre-long journey of each ray is irrelevant — only the microscopic leftover leg Δl = d·sinθ, cut off by a perpendicular right at the slits, decides whether P is bright or dark.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two constructions side by side on a white background, each with a small italic panel label (a) and (b) centered beneath. Left panel: a vertical tan/ochre bar at the left edge is the slit barrier with two small gaps labeled S₁ (upper) and S₂ (lower); a thin vertical double-arrow bracket to their left is labeled d. A gray vertical bar at the right is the screen, labeled 'Screen' at its top. A horizontal double-arrow bracket below spans barrier to screen, labeled D. Two teal rays rise from the slits to a black dot labeled P high on the screen, each with a mid-ray arrowhead and italic labels r₁ (upper) and r₂ (lower); short teal sine wave trains ride on each ray just past the slits. A black dashed horizontal runs from the slit midpoint to the screen, meeting it at the labeled point C, with a right-hand vertical double-arrow bracket labeled y from C up to P. A dashed line from the slit midpoint to P makes a small angle arc labeled θ with the dashed horizontal. Right panel: the same tan barrier and two slits with a d bracket at the left, but the two teal rays are now drawn parallel, each rising at the same angle θ, each ending in an arrowhead with the text 'to P'. Dashed horizontal reference lines emerge from each slit with θ arcs. A dashed line from the upper slit meets the lower ray at a small square right-angle marker; the short stretch of the lower ray between that foot and the lower slit is bracketed with a double arrow and labeled Δl, with an additional dashed segment closing the small right triangle below. Keep rays teal, barrier tan, screen gray, construction lines thin black dashes, labels serif italic. Add a compact live readout box (y, θ, d, Δl, Δl/λ) and a bright/dark indicator that changes color as Δl crosses integer and half-integer multiples of the wavelength. Δl should be drawn exaggerated for legibility while the readout reports honest physical values.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for screen point P height y: learner drags P up and down on the screen; rays r1 and r2 pivot, theta changes, and the extracted path difference delta l lengthens or shrinks in the side construction; the link between observation angle and interference path difference becomes clear.
- Slider for slit separation d: learner widens or narrows the gap between S1 and S2; the ray geometry and delta l segment update for the same screen point; the proportional relationship delta l = d sin(theta) becomes visible.
- Toggle between full apparatus and near-slit approximation: learner switches between the screen-scale view and the parallel-ray magnification; the long unequal paths collapse into the small right-triangle segment delta l; the approximation shows why only the extra path length controls constructive or destructive interference.

authoredContext:
The figure(a) shows how to determine the path length difference Δl for waves traveling from two slits to a common point on a screen. If the screen is a large distance away compared with the distance between the slits, then the angle θ between the path and a line from the slits to the screen [part (b)] is nearly the same for each path. In other words, r1 and r2 are essentially parallel. The lengths of r1 and r2 differ by Δl, as indicated by the two dashed lines in the figure. Simple trigonometry shows

where λ is the wavelength of the light, d is the distance between slits, and θ is the angle from the original direction of the beam as discussed above. We call m the order of the interference. For example, m=4 is fourth-order interference.

(a) To reach P, the light waves from S1 and S2 must travel different distances. (b) The path difference between the two rays is Δl.

Left picture is a schematic drawing that shows waves r1 and r2 passing through the two slits S1 and S2. The waves meet in a common point P on a screen. Distance between points S1 and S2 is d; distance between the screen with the two slits and the screen with point P is D. Point P is higher than the mid-point between S1 and S2 by the distance y. Imaginary line drawn from the point P to the mid-point between slits form an angle Theta with the x axis. Right picture is a schematic drawing that two slits separated by the distance d. Waves pass through the slits and travel to the screen P. Angle theta is formed by the travelling wave and x axis.

The equations for double-slit interference imply that a series of bright and dark lines are formed. For vertical slits, the light spreads out horizontally on either side of the incident beam into a pattern called interference fringes (the figure). The closer the slits are, the more the bright fringes spread apart. We can see this by examining the equation

discrepancies: A live readout card (y, θ, d, λ, Δl, Δl/λ, bright/dark verdict) is overlaid on the upper-left of panel (a); no such box exists in the source, and it occupies figure space that in the original is blank margin.

Overall label type size is noticeably smaller relative to the artwork than in the source (S₁, S₂, r₁, r₂, θ, d, D, y render at roughly 10 px effective at inline width), so the annotation hierarchy is flatter and harder to read than the original's prominent italic serif labels.

In panel (a) the θ arc/label sits very close to the two nearly-coincident dashed construction lines near the slit midpoint, producing local clutter that the source avoids by drawing a wider exaggerated angle.

Panel (b) proportions differ: the parallel rays are shorter and the little right triangle/Δl bracket is compressed compared with the source's large, clearly separated construction, and the '(b)' panel caption is off-centre relative to its drawing.

The guided tour opens on step 1 ('The apparatus', which specifies the (a)-only view) while the figure actually renders in 'Both side by side' mode, so the initial narration and the visible view are momentarily inconsistent.
evaluation.notes: A faithful two-panel reconstruction with correct barrier/screen/ray geometry, wave squiggles, all key labels (S₁, S₂, r₁, r₂, θ, y, d, D, P, C, Δl, 'to P') and strong, well-wired interactions (two sliders, view selector, 6-step tour, tooltips/popups); main weaknesses are undersized labels, an added live-readout overlay not in the source, and a slightly cramped panel (b) construction.
action_items: Increase annotation font sizes (~18-20 px in the 900×600 viewbox) and bold the primary symbols (r₁, r₂, d, D, y, θ, Δl) so the hierarchy matches the source at inline width.
Move the live readout card outside the drawing (e.g. into the side UI panel) or shrink/ghost it so it does not sit inside panel (a)'s frame.
Enlarge panel (b): lengthen the parallel rays, widen the θ exaggeration and the Δl bracket separation, and centre the '(b)' caption under its drawing.
Call applyStep(0) on load (or set the initial state/view to match step 1's narration) so the opening narration and rendered view agree.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (font sizes, overlay placement, panel (b) proportions, initial step sync) that the generator can fix directly.

discrepancies: Panel (a) default geometry is much flatter than the source: y is small so P sits only slightly above C and the rays r₁/r₂ nearly overlap, whereas the source shows a clearly separated fan with P high on the screen and a visibly large θ.

In panel (a) the θ arc/label, the dashed centre line, the dashed S-midpoint→P line, r₂ and the wave squiggles all collide in a small area near the slits, unlike the source where θ, r₁ and r₂ are cleanly separated.

Panel (b)'s ray inclination (~20°) is noticeably shallower than the source's ~45°, so the small right triangle and the Δl segment are more compressed and the perpendicular construction is less legible.
Wave squiggles in (a) are shorter and placed immediately at the slits; the source draws longer, more prominent sinusoids along a good fraction of each ray.

Extra chrome not in the source (live-value readout with λ, Δl/λ and a bright/dark status line) sits in the side panel — acceptable, but it introduces quantities (λ = 550 nm, m order) not present in the original figure.
evaluation.notes: A faithful two-panel reproduction with correct primitives (barrier, screen, teal rays with arrowheads, dashed constructions, d/y/D/Δl brackets, right-angle mark) and genuinely useful interactions (two sliders, a view selector, and a six-step guided tour), weakened mainly by a flattened default geometry in (a) and label crowding around the θ/r₂ region near the slits.

feedback.rationale: Concept, panels, and interactions are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (default geometry too flat, ray angle, label crowding, squiggle length) best fixed in rendering.

plan.concept: For two-slit interference, the only thing that determines whether light arriving at a point P on the screen interferes constructively or destructively is the tiny extra path length Δl = d·sinθ travelled by the far slit's ray, not the individual path lengths r₁ and r₂.

interactions.teaches: Moving the observation point P up the screen increases the angle θ, which in turn lengthens the extra path Δl — so position on the screen and path difference are two views of the same quantity.
interactions.label: Height of P on screen, y (mm)

interactions.teaches: For a fixed viewing angle, widening the slits scales the extra path length in direct proportion, making Δl = d·sinθ visible as a geometric fact rather than a formula.
interactions.label: Slit separation d (µm)

interactions.teaches: The full apparatus shows two long, slightly unequal paths; the near-slit magnification shows that their entire difference is captured by one short right-triangle leg — the far-field approximation that makes interference tractable.
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Each geometric quantity (d, D, y, θ, r₁, r₂, Δl) names a specific segment or angle in the construction, so the symbols in the formula map onto real pieces of the picture.

demo_steps.title: The apparatus
demo_steps.narration: Light leaves two slits separated by d and travels a distance D to the screen. Choose a point P a height y above the center point C; the rays r₁ and r₂ reach it along slightly different paths.

demo_steps.title: Slide P up the screen
demo_steps.narration: Drag P upward. The angle θ between the center line and the line to P grows, and r₁ becomes noticeably shorter than r₂ — but the difference is far too small to see at this scale.

demo_steps.title: Zoom in on the slits
demo_steps.narration: Because D is enormous compared with d, the two rays to P are essentially parallel. Dropping a perpendicular from the upper slit onto the lower ray isolates the whole difference in one short segment, Δl.

demo_steps.title: Read the right triangle
demo_steps.narration: The triangle has hypotenuse d and the angle at the slit equals θ, so the isolated leg is exactly Δl = d·sinθ. Watch it shrink as you move P back toward the center.

demo_steps.title: Widen the slits
demo_steps.narration: Hold the angle and widen d: Δl grows in direct proportion, so more bright fringes are packed into the same span of screen.

demo_steps.title: Both views at once
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, a screen-scale change in y and a micron-scale change in Δl move together. Whenever Δl is a whole number of wavelengths the waves arrive in phase and P is bright; a half-integer gives darkness.

plan.keyInsight: The kilometre-long journey of each ray is irrelevant — only the microscopic leftover leg Δl = d·sinθ, cut off by a perpendicular right at the slits, decides whether P is bright or dark.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two constructions side by side on a white background, each with a small italic panel label (a) and (b) centered beneath. Left panel: a vertical tan/ochre bar at the left edge is the slit barrier with two small gaps labeled S₁ (upper) and S₂ (lower); a thin vertical double-arrow bracket to their left is labeled d. A gray vertical bar at the right is the screen, labeled 'Screen' at its top. A horizontal double-arrow bracket below spans barrier to screen, labeled D. Two teal rays rise from the slits to a black dot labeled P high on the screen, each with a mid-ray arrowhead and italic labels r₁ (upper) and r₂ (lower); short teal sine wave trains ride on each ray just past the slits. A black dashed horizontal runs from the slit midpoint to the screen, meeting it at the labeled point C, with a right-hand vertical double-arrow bracket labeled y from C up to P. A dashed line from the slit midpoint to P makes a small angle arc labeled θ with the dashed horizontal. Right panel: the same tan barrier and two slits with a d bracket at the left, but the two teal rays are now drawn parallel, each rising at the same angle θ, each ending in an arrowhead with the text 'to P'. Dashed horizontal reference lines emerge from each slit with θ arcs. A dashed line from the upper slit meets the lower ray at a small square right-angle marker; the short stretch of the lower ray between that foot and the lower slit is bracketed with a double arrow and labeled Δl, with an additional dashed segment closing the small right triangle below. Keep rays teal, barrier tan, screen gray, construction lines thin black dashes, labels serif italic. Add a compact live readout box (y, θ, d, Δl, Δl/λ) and a bright/dark indicator that changes color as Δl crosses integer and half-integer multiples of the wavelength. Δl should be drawn exaggerated for legibility while the readout reports honest physical values.

discrepancies: Default 'Both side by side' view squeezes the 920-unit-wide drawing into roughly half the page width, so every text label (S₁, S₂, r₁, r₂, C, P, θ, Δl, 'Screen', 'to P') renders at ~9–10 px and is uncomfortably small compared with the clearly legible type in the source.

In panel (a) the wave squiggles are drawn as thin low-amplitude sinusoids running along a long stretch of each ray, whereas the source shows short, large-amplitude loopy wave trains near the slits — the visual cue for 'light waves' is much weaker.

Panel (b)'s right-angle tick and the perpendicular dashed construction are drawn very small/faint relative to the source, where the perpendicular from the leading slit and its square mark are a prominent part of the construction.
The θ label in panel (a) sits noticeably outside/above its arc (arc radius 42, label radius 52), and the r₁ label crowds the wave train on the upper ray, unlike the clean placements in the source.
Demo step 5 narrates 'Hold the angle and widen d' but simultaneously changes y from 3 to 8 mm, so θ is not held constant — the stated relationship is not what the figure demonstrates.
evaluation.notes: Structurally a faithful two-panel reproduction of the double-slit geometry with correct Δl = d·sinθ physics and a rich, functional set of interactions (two sliders, view selector, 6-step tour, tooltips/popups), but the default side-by-side view shrinks all annotations to barely legible size and a few labels (θ, r₁) sit awkwardly relative to their marks.
action_items: Increase label font sizes (or scale the viewBox per view) so text remains ~13–14 px effective in the default 'Both side by side' state; consider making the figure area wider relative to the UI panel.

Redraw the panel-(a) wave trains as short, large-amplitude loops near the slits to match the source's wave-source cue, and enlarge the panel-(b) right-angle tick and perpendicular so the construction reads clearly.
Nudge the θ label inside its arc in panel (a) and offset r₁ further from the wave train to avoid crowding.
Fix demo step 5 so it changes only d (keeping y/θ fixed) to genuinely demonstrate Δl ∝ d.
